Also called manriki-gusari or rante: a length of chain weighted at each end. Whirled fast, it strikes hard blows with the weights. One end can be swung out to entangle a foe, or the whole chain thrown like a bola to entangle and hurt at once. It is popular where a lord has banned other weapons, or where secrecy is needed, since it can be worn as a belt or hidden under a sash. Ninja use it often for its many uses.

A single-edged, slightly curved sword ending in a chisel point, perhaps one of the finest swords ever made. Forging one is a rare and prized art: the smith labors long hours for the right temper, and a well-made blade is light, balanced, strong, flexible and resilient, and takes a razor edge. Blades are often etched with designs, prayers or family lineages, and the hilt, guard and scabbard get equal care. Katanas often have names recalling glorious deeds they were used in.

To a samurai, the katana is part of who he is: his personal weapon, not for others. Touching the scabbard of his sheathed katana, or drawing the blade without permission, insults him. A katana may be a family heirloom for generations, and losing one is a disgrace wiped clean only by recovering it and punishing the takers; many samurai have died trying.

The listed price is for an average blade; others cost more or less with their quality, workmanship and history. See also The Katana and the Daisho in the OA Lite journals.

The lasso does no damage. A hit means it has settled around a man-sized or smaller victim, who is entangled.

  • A victim with intelligence above 2 and a way to cut the rope saves versus poison; success means he has freed himself.
  • A mounted victim without horsemanship is dismounted automatically; one with it rolls against his proficiency.
  • A two-legged creature on foot weighing no more than half the lasso user's weight is pulled off its feet 25% of the time. Several creatures pulling on the rope together add 20% each, and the reverse.
  • The rope takes 2 points of cutting damage, and a victim can break it with a successful bend bars roll, one try per character.

A two-pronged pole arm, each prong curved to close around a man-sized humanoid. Creatures 50% or more larger or smaller than man-sized are unaffected. Spikes and sharp edges hurt the victim and stop him using his hands and arms.

  • A caught victim loses all shield and dexterity bonuses.
  • He can be pushed and pulled with it, taking 1-2 damage a round automatically, with a 25% chance of being pulled off his feet to kneeling or prone.
  • He can break free with a successful bend bars roll, and may keep trying, but takes 1-4 damage each try unless wearing heavy gloves or gauntlets.
  • Others can rescue him by chopping through the haft (6 points of cutting damage).
  • A common tactic is to catch the victim, jerk him off his feet or horse, and press the pole down to pin his neck to the ground, leaving him almost helpless.

The DM can allow other hidden devices.

Used only to catch, it does no damage, but it can also strike forcefully, with the same effect and the listed damage. Palace guards and city constables often carry it.

Small caltrops: balls or four-sided spiked shapes that always land with a spike up. They aren't melee or thrown weapons; they are scattered at the feet of pursuers to make the ground dangerous to cross. Ninja favor them for quick, unpursued escapes.

  • The user says how many he scatters and over what area. The base is 10 in a 5-foot square (25 square feet).
  • Anyone entering saves versus paralyzation. On a failure he steps on one, takes 1-4 damage and must stop.
  • With half the base number, the save is at +4. Each 5 over the base 10 gives -2 on the save and +1 damage (up to +6).
  • Moving faster than half normal speed gives -2 on the save. Check once for each 5-foot section entered. Moving cautiously (1/3 speed) needs no saves.
  • A creature that steps on one must spend a round pulling it out before moving on, then saves versus paralyzation again: on a failure it is lamed and moves at 1/3 speed for 24 hours or until the damage is healed.

A short sword made like the katana, which may also be named for some past deed. It holds almost as important a place for a samurai as his katana, and when part of a matched set it is treated the same way. Worn together, katana and wakizashi are the daisho ("long and short"); in many lands only samurai may wear both, and others who do can be arrested or executed on the spot. See The Katana and the Daisho in the OA Lite journals.

To do damage, a whip must strike bare or lightly covered skin. Heavy clothing, thick hair or fur protects well until torn away by repeated lashes. Thick hide like an elephant's or rhinoceros's feels at most a slight sting and takes no real damage, and heavily scaled or armored creatures don't even feel it, even with a weighted tip. A whip can also entangle, often more usefully than it does damage.

A repeating light crossbow. A magazine on top holds up to 10 quarrels, and a single lever, pushed forward and pulled back, cocks and reloads it, so it fires faster than a normal crossbow.

  • Two quarrels can be loaded into the magazine per round, so a full reload takes five rounds.
  • It can't fire and reload in the same round.
  • It is heavier than a normal crossbow and has a shorter range.

A small wooden blower with a mouthpiece, a powder chamber and a tube. Blowing hard puffs the powder out, perhaps into the victim's face. It does no damage but blows irritating or blinding powders, most often pepper, ashes or dust. On a hit the victim saves versus poison or is helpless for 1-6 rounds. Ninja use it to distract and escape, and city constables when catching criminals. (Its range is printed as 3', with the note that the range is in tens of feet.)

Hardly an effective weapon, but ninja sometimes carry needles for distraction or surprise, up to 20 in the mouth, fired by spitting or blowing (using the tongue as a blowpipe).

  • Fired one at a time, each needle needs a normal to-hit roll and does 1 point of damage.
  • Fired in a burst, roll the die equal to the number fired for damage: all 20 at once do 1d20.
  • Needles carried in the mouth can't be poisoned, have very poor range and almost never work against any armor, but they surprise and distract, being hidden.
  • Needles aren't usually considered an honorable weapon.

A small shield strapped to the arm near the fist; it can be worn while using a weapon in the same hand. It counts as a small shield. Horse nomads use bucklers often.

Rings of metal woven or pinned together, easily tailored to almost any shape and put to many uses: horse nomads sometimes wear chain helmets and vests, kote are made of it, and ninja and nobles alike wear chain suits. Worn under clothing it is hard to detect.

Armor piece: improves armor class by 2 step(s) from AC 10 (OA Table 53). Pieces add together (e.g. kote, do-maru and haidate give AC 6); the sheet counts only the best single item, so enter the combined total as an armor class override or misc adjustment. Pieces cannot be worn with suits of armor; only one piece per body area.

A corselet covering the stomach, chest, shoulders and back, with small tassets hanging over the waist and upper legs that can overlap the haidate. It may be plain or elaborate, and is usually laced armor.

Armor of the hide of especially thick-skinned animals, most often elephant or rhinoceros, giving better protection than ordinary leather.

OA p.39, 48-49 (Tables 47, 52-54).

Armor piece: improves armor class by 1 step(s) from AC 10 (OA Table 53). Pieces add together (e.g. kote, do-maru and haidate give AC 6); the sheet counts only the best single item, so enter the combined total as an armor class override or misc adjustment. Pieces cannot be worn with suits of armor; only one piece per body area.

A pair of armored sleeves joined by a band of leather or cloth across the shoulders, running from the shoulders to the backs of the hands. Usually mail, some with small metal plates sewn in, from very plain to highly decorated. Kote can be worn inconspicuously under robes and combined with other pieces.

OA p.39, 48-49 (Tables 47, 52-54).

Armor class 3, as printed on Table 52 ("o-yori").

A complete matched suit of laced armor: kote, do-maru, sode, haidate, kabuto and sune-ate, plus smaller pieces including the mempo (face mask), nodawa (neck guard), wakibiki (armpit guards), and the sendan-no-ita and hato-wo-no-ita (guards for the front of the armpits). Being made as a set, with matching colors and patterns, it fits better and gives a better armor class than unmatched pieces. Costly and highly decorative, o-yoroi are worn for ceremonies and major battles, seldom every day.

OA p.39, 48-49 (Tables 47, 52-54).

Thick pieces of hardened leather sewn to cloth or leather, each overlapping its neighbors, worn by common soldiers and horsemen.

OA p.39, 48-49 (Tables 47, 52-54).

Made like leather scale but of metal, and far less common; usually worn by wealthier or more important warriors.

OA p.39, 48-49 (Tables 47, 52-54).

Whether shields are used depends on the land; in some, never. Nearly all are lighter than the shields of the PHB: woven bamboo and wicker, stretched and hardened leather, or thick layers of coconut fiber or hemp. Metal-edged wooden shields are extremely rare.

In battle a cloth (sode jiruchi) dyed or painted with the wearer's badge is sometimes tied over them.

Shin guards from the ankle to below the knee, usually metal splints on leather padding wrapped around and tied, protecting against crippling blows to the lower leg.

OA p.39, 48-49 (Tables 47, 52-54).

A simple helmet of hardened leather or light metal plates that fits the head snugly. Some cover only the crown and forehead; others the whole head and ears. Small, light, collapsible, cheap and undecorated, they are often worn by common soldiers. The book gives it no armor class effect.

OA p.39, 49.

On the price list (1 gp), but the book doesn't describe it or give it an armor class effect.

OA p.39, 49.

Long strips of cloth sewn together, tied at the neck and near the waist, worn by some mounted warriors. When riding, it fills with wind and balloons out behind; worn this way it works only while riding, but a wicker frame underneath makes it work at all times. It improves the wearer's armor class by 1 against missiles shot at his back only, and has no other protective use. Usually brightly colored and bearing the owner's crest, it identifies the rider's family and shows he is no common soldier.

OA p.39, 49.

An iron version of the peasant's round straw hat, worn by common soldiers, with no guards for ears, cheeks or neck. It is popular because it doubles as a cooking pot on campaign. The book gives it no armor class effect.

OA p.39, 49.

The great helmet often worn with the o-yoroi. Its bowl is iron strips riveted together, often with a small opening at the top where they meet. A flaring neck guard hangs at the back and sides, usually curving out in two wings at the front, and elaborate crests are mounted in front: horns, antlers, leaping fish, half-moons. Red silk cords hold it on. One of the most visible parts of a warrior's armor, it is often fancifully shaped (demon faces, seashells, fists holding thunderbolts, tall cones, fish, wild animals), sometimes covered with human hair or fur, its bowl decorated with silver, copper and gold, its neck guard laced outside and lined with dyed or painted leather.

The kabuto gives armor class 3 to the wearer's head.
